conflict_topics: fair access to stove on weeknights / scheduling

Some repetition: A restated the chat/stove rule twice across rounds (Turns 10 and 13).
C's chore complaint reappeared late in the transcript and was not addressed, creating an unresolved item.
evaluation.final_reason: Partial settlements achieved: Agent A agreed to and enacted extractor/window use to reduce smells (Agent A: "I'll turn the extractor on and open the window now.") and proposed/clarified a stove-access rule that D accepted: first-come-first-served with a chat post to reserve or swap (Agent A: "weeknights, first come first served... post in the chat"; Agent A: "Yes. Post in the chat and if no one says they need the stove...go ahead and cook that night."). The shared-chore conflict was not resolved: Agent C demanded the pan be washed now and nobody admitted or washed it (Agent C: "Who used that pan last night? Can you wash it now — we agreed the user should clean pans the same night.").
position_change_notes: Agent A proposed rules and conceded to immediate actions (turned extractor on) — moved from being called out to offering fixes.
Agent D shifted from complaint about fairness to acceptance of A's proposed first-come-first-served plus chat procedure.
Agent C remained consistent in demanding cleaning of the shared pan; this position was not accommodated in the transcript.
Agent B accepted A's initial proposal quickly and did not change position thereafter.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A proposed concrete household rules (wash pans same night; use extractor; close bedroom doors) and asked to be told directly: "Whoever uses a pan washes it the same night. I’ll always use the extractor and open the window..." Agent B accepted: "Okay, sounds fair." This reduced immediate tension but multiple issues (unwashed pan, fair stove access) remained unsettled.

Agent C prompted A to follow the agreed extractor/window action: "Agent A — you said you'd use the extractor and open the window on weeknights. Can you do that now?" Agent A complied: "Okay, I'll turn the extractor on and open the window now." The smell issue was acted on, but the unwashed pan and stove-access arrangements remained unresolved.

Agent D introduced a new, substantive practical conflict about fair stove access: "Can we agree on a simple weeknight rule so everyone gets a chance to use the stove? I get home late and should have a fair shot." Agent A proposed a rule (first come, first served; post in chat to swap): "weeknights, first come first served... post in the chat and we'll swap or let you cook that night." This is a clear expressed incompatibility in practical interests; a proposed solution was offered but not yet accepted by all.

D sought clarification about the chat rule and A confirmed the practical procedure: "Yes. Post in the chat and if no one says they need the stove and it's not already in use, go ahead and cook that night." The stove-access conflict was clarified and functionally settled for late arrivals, but other issues (unwashed pan) remained.

A repeated the chat rule and D agreed to try it: "Yes. Post in the chat; if no one says they need the stove and it's not already in use, go ahead and cook that night." / "Okay, fair. I'll post in the chat when I'm late and try this for a week." This reiterated an already-clarified arrangement; the unresolved chore issue (pan) persisted.

Agent C directly re-raised the unwashed-pan chore conflict and demanded immediate compliance: "Who used that pan last night? Can you wash it now — we agreed the user should clean pans the same night." There is no recorded compliance or admission, so this substantive dispute about chores remains active and reopened attention.

substantive_insights: Participants converged on practical, low-friction solutions for smells (use extractor/open window) and stove scheduling (first-come-first-served + chat), showing preference for simple, trial-period rules.
The cleaning/chore norm (user washes pan same night) was stated as an expectation but enforcement and immediate compliance were never secured, leaving recurring friction.
Clarifying who is expected to act (e.g., post in chat, if no reply you may cook) helped resolve procedural ambiguity for one primary conflict (stove access).
